sections.h2: What notice must a New Jersey landlord give before filing an eviction?
sections.html:
It depends on the reason. Under the Anti-Eviction Act, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 and following, a landlord who wants a judgment for possession of a New Jersey rental generally must make a written demand and give written notice first, and the length of that notice runs from three days to three years. Unpaid rent is the main exception.

The Department of Community Affairs summarizes the rule in its Landlord-Tenant Information Service bulletin: every good cause eviction other than nonpayment needs a written Notice to Quit that describes the cause. A Notice to Quit ends the tenancy on paper, but the tenant does not have to leave until a court enters a judgment for possession.

For an owner thinking about selling a rented house, the order matters. The notice period has to run before the complaint is filed, so a sale timeline that depends on a vacant house has to start with the correct notice on the correct date.

sections.h2: Does a New Jersey landlord need a notice before suing for unpaid rent?
sections.html:
No, with one common exception. Nonpayment of rent is ground a. of N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1, and N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2 excuses the written demand and notice for that ground. The landlord can file in the Special Civil Part right away.

The DCA bulletin adds that a tenant in federally subsidized housing is owed a 14-day notice before suit. It also says a tenant cannot be evicted for nonpayment when the unpaid portion of rent went to keep electric, gas, water or sewer service on after the utility warned of shutoff because the landlord had not paid it.

A tenant who owes rent keeps a way out even after suit begins. The NJ Courts landlord-tenant page says the case may be dismissed if the tenant pays all rent due plus court costs by 4:30 p.m. on the trial date.

sections.h2: How many days or months of notice does each ground require?
sections.html:
The statute sets the minimum for each ground, and the table pulls the common ones together. A court can reject a complaint if the landlord gave a shorter notice than the ground requires, so the count matters.

Minimum notice before filing, from N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2 as reprinted by the NJ Department of Community Affairs
GroundSubsection of 2A:18-61.1Notice before suit
Disorderly conduct, property damage, drug or assault offenses, theft findingsb, c, m, n, o, p3 days
Rule violations, lease covenant breach, habitual late rentd, e, j1 month
Refusing reasonable new lease termsi1 month
Unpaid rent increase after valid noticef1 month
Owner or buyer will occupy (three units or fewer)l2 months, after the lease ends
Board-up, demolition or code complianceg3 months
Permanent retirement from residential useh18 months, after the lease ends
Condominium or co-op conversionk3 years, after the lease ends

For the one-month grounds, the DCA bulletin also says the notice should be given on or before the start of a new month.

sections.h2: What does a Notice to Cease do, and how is it different from a Notice to Quit?
sections.html:
A Notice to Cease is a warning, and a Notice to Quit is the step that ends the tenancy. Several grounds require both, in that order.

  • Notice to Cease: tells the tenant to stop the conduct, such as disorderly behavior, breaking house rules, or paying late again and again.
  • Notice to Quit: follows if the conduct continues, and it starts the clock for the 3-day or 1-month period in the table.
  • Notice of rent increase: for a rent increase dispute, the landlord must serve a valid Notice to Quit together with notice of the increase before suing over the unpaid amount.

The DCA bulletin notes that courts treat habitual late payment as more than one late payment after the Notice to Cease. It also says a landlord who keeps accepting late rent has to keep warning the tenant that further late payments will lead to eviction, or the original warning can be treated as waived.

sections.h2: What must the notice say, and how can it be delivered?
sections.html:
The notice must state the cause of termination in detail. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2 says that for every ground it covers, the notice shall specify in detail the cause, so a vague line about breaking the lease is a weak foundation for a case.

Delivery has three accepted routes in the reprinted statute.

  • Hand a copy to the tenant or person in possession.
  • Leave a copy at the tenant's usual home with a family member older than 14.
  • Send it by certified mail, and if the certified letter is not claimed, follow with regular mail.

The NJ Courts self-help page adds that, for any case other than unpaid rent, the landlord must attach every notice sent to the tenant to the verified complaint when filing. A landlord who skipped a required notice will have nothing to attach.

sections.h2: Which New Jersey rentals fall outside these notice rules?
sections.html:
The Anti-Eviction Act does not cover every rental. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 carves out owner-occupied premises with no more than two rental units, hotels, motels and guesthouses rented to transient guests or seasonal tenants, and certain units held for a family member with a developmental disability.

Those cases fall under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53 instead, the same statute the NJ Courts site points to for commercial tenants. For a disorderly tenant or one who destroys or damages the property, that older statute calls for a written notice demanding the tenant leave within three days of service. Holdover cases after a lease ends need a demand and written notice for delivery of possession.

A landlord who owns a two-family house and lives upstairs is therefore working under a different notice scheme than the owner of a three-unit building who lives elsewhere. Confirm which statute applies before serving anything.

sections.h2: Can a landlord raise the rent or change lease terms with a notice?
sections.html:
Yes, but not in the middle of a lease term. The DCA Truth in Renting guide says New Jersey has no statewide rent control, and that a landlord who wants to raise rent must end the old lease and offer a new one at the higher rent, with written notice that the tenant may stay by signing it.

Local law can add limits. The guide says a municipality may adopt a rent control or rent leveling ordinance and that the town's rent control board or municipal clerk can say whether a unit is covered. It also says an increase cannot be unconscionable, a fact-based test that looks at the size of the increase, the landlord's expenses, and rents for similar properties nearby.

The grounds list in 2A:18-61.1 also lets a landlord seek removal of a tenant who refuses reasonable changes to lease terms at renewal, after written notice and the one-month period.

sections.h2: What notice applies when the owner or a buyer wants to move in?
sections.html:
Two months, and only after the lease expires. Subsection l.(3) of N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 lets the owner of a building with three residential units or fewer seek possession to occupy a unit, or because a contract of sale calls for the unit to be vacant at closing and the buyer will live there.

The DCA bulletin sets the notice for that ground at two months before suit, with no action until the lease runs out. The same pattern applies to some condominium and co-op units. A tenant who vacates on this kind of notice has a damages claim if the owner then fails to occupy for at least six months, since N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.6 allows treble damages plus attorney fees in that situation.

Sellers of larger rented buildings and sellers who want the house empty for an investor buyer do not get this shortcut. For them, the tenancy continues until one of the listed grounds is proved in court.

sections.h2: What happens to a tenant's notice rights when the house is sold?
sections.html:
They carry over to the new owner. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.3(b) says a tenant covered by the Act cannot be removed by the landlord's successor in ownership except for good cause, a federal-law override, or an eminent domain or code enforcement proceeding.

The NJ Courts site adds that a landlord must notify the tenant in writing about the security deposit account, including when ownership or control of the property transfers. The deposit itself, capped at one and a half months of rent, stays tied to the tenancy.

A buyer purchasing a tenant-occupied house is buying that tenancy with it. Buyers who want a vacant property can offer the tenant a negotiated move-out, but New Jersey requires the tenant to leave only through a court judgment and a Special Civil Part officer.

faqs.q: Is a verbal notice enough to start an eviction in New Jersey?
faqs.a: No. The Anti-Eviction Act calls for written demand and written notice, delivered by hand, left at the tenant's home with a family member over 14, or sent by certified mail. A landlord without a written notice has nothing to attach to the complaint.

faqs.q: Can a landlord evict without any notice for unpaid rent?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. Nonpayment is excused from the written notice requirement in N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2. The exception in the DCA bulletin is federally subsidized housing, which needs a 14-day notice before suit.

faqs.q: Does a 3-day notice mean the tenant must leave in 3 days?
faqs.a: No. The 3 days is the minimum wait before the landlord may file suit on grounds such as disorderly conduct or damage. The tenant stays until a judge enters a judgment for possession and a court officer carries out a warrant of removal.

faqs.q: How long does a landlord have to wait to evict a tenant for habitual late rent?
faqs.a: One month. After a written Notice to Cease and continued late payment, the landlord serves a Notice to Quit and waits one month before filing, according to the DCA grounds bulletin and 2A:18-61.2.

faqs.q: Can a landlord evict a tenant because the owner is selling the house?
faqs.a: Only in narrow cases. A building with three residential units or fewer can be cleared on two months' notice if the buyer will live there and the contract calls for a vacant unit. Otherwise a sale alone is not good cause, and the buyer takes the property subject to the tenancy.
